To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
CO(2)-induced benefits in wheat were diminished in high O(3), but not in corn.
CO(2)-induced benefits in wheat grain yield were diminished by O(3)-stress, whereas O(3)-damage in wheat and corn grain yield were not diminished by CO(2) enhancement.

1) CO(3) enrichment had beneficial effects in wheat, but not in corn; 2) high O(3), but not CO(2), exposure reduced wheat and corn yields; 3) no significant interactive effects of CO(3) and O(3), averaged over the two years of study, were observed in wheat and corn; and 4) O(3)- and CO(2)-induced effects on crop yields were similar in magnitude.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effects of enhanced O(3) and CO(2) on crop growth and productivity, and the results indicate that the O(2) concentration in the atmosphere is likely to be the major limiting factor on crop production.

the effects of elevated CO(2) and O(3)-stress are additive in nature.
the beneficial effect of elevated CO(2) on wheat yield is not likely to be realized in the coming century, when the atmospheric O(3) levels are expected to increase.
the beneficial effects of increased CO(2) will be partially offset by the negative effects of increased O(3).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of CO(3) enrichment in wheat and corn were positive, whereas O(3) stress had a negative effect on both crops.
the combined effects of CO( 2) enrichment and elevated O(3) levels will have a negative impact on crop yield and dry biomass in both wheat and corn.
the combined effects of CO(3) enrichment and O3 stress on crop yield and biomass were not additive.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combined effect of elevated O(3) and CO(2) on wheat yield was less than the additive effects of the individual treatments.
the effects of elevated CO(2) on crop yield and biomass are likely to be offset by the detrimental effects of increased O(3) concentrations.
O(3) and CO(2) interact in a complex manner and the effects on crop production are difficult to predict.
